Module 3 — Single-Species Occupancy

Snapshot Brasil multi-network camera-trap pipeline

What this module covers

Single-species occupancy models estimate the probability that a species is present at a site (3c8, “psi”), separately from the probability that we detect it given it is present (p). This module builds up from one species and one model to the full community, then works through two extensions: letting a habitat effect depend on temperature, and letting it depend on ecoregion.

Two different covariate sets are used, chosen in Module 2: an 11-covariate camera-level set (forest, savanna, pasture, cropland, landscape-scale native vegetation, temperature, precipitation, built-surface extent, distance to road, distance to water, plus protected-area status) for models fit at the camera level, and a leaner 6-covariate array-level set (a data-driven reduction of the same candidates) for the one place in this module where the sampling unit is collapsed to the array. Every species-level model uses the range-mask candidate site set from Module 2’s range-map evaluation: sites outside a species’ mapped range that were never detected there are excluded by default; sites detected outside the mapped range are always kept.

ds <- fread(file.path(DATA, "dataset_summary.csv"))

1 A first occupancy model: Nine-banded Armadillo

We start with the Nine-banded Armadillo (Dasypus novemcinctus), a well-detected species, and fit a model using every covariate in the 11-covariate camera-level set: forest, savanna, pasture, cropland, landscape-scale native vegetation, temperature, precipitation, built-surface extent, distance to road, distance to water, and protected-area status.

arm_n <- fread(file.path(DATA, "armadillo_candidate_sites.csv"))

1.1 Detection history

Occupancy models are built from a detection history: for each 7-day occasion, was the species detected (1), not detected (0), or was the camera not running (missing)? The picture below shows two contrasting arrays: one with many detections, one with almost none.

knitr::include_graphics(file.path(FIGS, "m3_dethist_armadillo.png"))

1.2 Fitting the model, with the array random effect

We fit the model with a random intercept per array — the pipeline’s standard correction for pseudoreplication among cameras that share the same array (see Module 2). Because this is a random-effects model, we use a Bayesian engine (spOccupancy::PGOcc) rather than the maximum-likelihood unmarked package, which only fits fixed effects.

pg <- fread(file.path(DATA, "armadillo_pgocc_coefs.csv"))
knitr::kable(pg[param != "(Intercept)"], digits=3,
  caption="Nine-banded Armadillo occupancy model, array random effect included, 11-covariate camera-level set (posterior mean, and 95% credible interval).")
Nine-banded Armadillo occupancy model, array random effect included, 11-covariate camera-level set (posterior mean, and 95% credible interval).

savanna_100m_z 0.484 -0.264 1.149
pasture_100m_z 0.023 -0.302 0.341
cropland_100m_z 0.155 -0.156 0.460

1.3 Naive vs. modeled occupancy

“Naive occupancy” is simply the fraction of sites where the species was ever detected — it always underestimates true occupancy, because a species can be present but missed on every visit.

knitr::include_graphics(file.path(FIGS, "m3_naive_vs_modeled.png"))

1.4 Covariate effects

The panel below shows predicted occupancy against the covariate with a credible effect in the array random-effect fit, holding the others at their mean.

knitr::include_graphics(file.path(FIGS, "m3_armadillo_effect_curves.png"))
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(FIGS, "m3_armadillo_beta_ci.png"))

1.5 Model fit: what do these numbers actually mean?

Two very different questions get asked of a fitted occupancy model:

  • Does the model discriminate occupied sites from unoccupied ones? — AUC. Take the model’s predicted occupancy probability at every site and ask: if you picked one truly-occupied site and one truly-unoccupied site at random, how often would the model give the occupied one a higher predicted probability? AUC = 0.5 is chance; AUC = 1.0 is perfect.
  • Is the assumed error structure correct? — c-hat (overdispersion), from a parametric-bootstrap goodness-of-fit test. c-hat near 1 means the assumed binomial detection process fits; notably above 1 means real detections are more variable than the model expects. AUC and c-hat are not interchangeable — a model can discriminate well (high AUC) and still be overdispersed.
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(FIGS, "m3_auc_explainer.png"))
fs <- fread(file.path(DATA, "armadillo_fit_summary.csv"))
knitr::kable(fs, digits=3, col.names=c("AUC","c-hat","Bootstrap GoF p-value","Detection probability"),
  caption="Model-fit diagnostics for the Nine-banded Armadillo array-RE fit.")
Model-fit diagnostics for the Nine-banded Armadillo array-RE fit.
AUC c-hat Bootstrap GoF p-value Detection probability
0.672 1.609 0 0.193

An AUC around 0.65 indicates modest discrimination — better than chance, but far from perfect, which is typical for occupancy models built on binary detection data. A c-hat above 1 means the model is overdispersed relative to the assumed binomial detection process — both common, expected findings, not a sign the model is unusable.

1.6 Does adding protected-area status improve the model?

pa <- fread(file.path(DATA, "armadillo_pa_effect.csv"))
knitr::kable(pa, digits=3, col.names=c("\u0394AIC","Direction","\u03c8 outside PA","\u03c8 inside PA","Ratio (in / out)"),
  caption="AIC improvement from adding protected-area status, and predicted occupancy inside vs. outside protected areas, other covariates held at their mean.")
AIC improvement from adding protected-area status, and predicted occupancy inside vs. outside protected areas, other covariates held at their mean.
ΔAIC Direction ψ outside PA ψ inside PA Ratio (in / out)
21.8 negative 0.369 0.183 0.5

Adding in_pa produces a decisive AIC improvement. The direction of the effect is negative: Armadillo occupancy is lower inside protected areas. In concrete terms, predicted occupancy inside protected areas is roughly half of predicted occupancy outside — a substantial effect, not just a statistically detectable one.

2 Every species, together

We go straight to the array random-effect model for the community fit — a fixed-effects-only engine is unreliable for roughly half the community (quasi-complete separation, standard errors well above 5, usually because one land-cover class is close to zero at nearly every detection site).

cfc <- fread(file.path(DATA, "community_fit_count.csv"))
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(FIGS, "m3_beta_shaded_table.png"))

Forest is the most consistently important covariate across the community, positive for the great majority of species with a credible effect.

2.1 Does the array-level simplification hold?

Module 2 flagged that habitat is not always homogeneous within an array. We test directly: does using arrays — rather than individual cameras — as the sampling unit change the ecological conclusions? This is now a comparison of two genuinely different covariate sets, not just two sampling levels with the same covariates: the camera-level fit uses the full 11-covariate set (1,110+ sites easily supports this); the array-level fit uses the reduced 6-covariate set (60 arrays cannot support more; see Module 2 for how that set was chosen).

Six species illustrate the comparison: Spotted Paca and Nine-banded Armadillo (data-rich), White-lipped Peccary (sparser, range-masked), and Ocelot, Lowland Tapir, and Puma (chosen for large camera-vs-array shifts).

ac <- fread(file.path(DATA, "array_completeness.csv"))

60 of 61 arrays have complete covariate data for array-level models — one array has no valid camera-level habitat data on any of its cameras and is dropped rather than silently carried as an undefined average.

knitr::include_graphics(file.path(FIGS, "m3_array_vs_site_6species.png"))
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(FIGS, "m3_camera_vs_array_fit_6species.png"))
fst <- fread(file.path(DATA, "fitstats_6species.csv"))
common_lookup6 <- c("Cuniculus paca"="Spotted Paca","Dasypus novemcinctus"="Nine-banded Armadillo",
                    "Tayassu pecari"="White-lipped Peccary","Leopardus pardalis"="Ocelot",
                    "Tapirus terrestris"="Lowland Tapir","Puma concolor"="Puma")
fst[, common := common_lookup6[species]]
knitr::kable(fst[, .(common, n_site, n_array, auc_site, auc_array)], digits=3,
  col.names=c("Species","N (camera-level)","N (array-level)","AUC (camera, 11 cov.)","AUC (array, 6 cov.)"),
  caption="Camera-level vs. array-level model-fit statistics, six species.")
Camera-level vs. array-level model-fit statistics, six species.
Species N (camera-level) N (array-level) AUC (camera, 11 cov.) AUC (array, 6 cov.)
Spotted Paca 1110 60 0.737 0.824
Nine-banded Armadillo 1110 60 0.672 0.679
White-lipped Peccary 838 44 0.929 0.766
Ocelot 1110 60 0.625 0.815
Lowland Tapir 1007 53 0.839 0.743
Puma 1110 60 0.767 0.790

Note that the camera-level model also carries four covariates — built-surface extent, distance to road, distance to water, protected-area status — that the array-level model has no room to include; the coefficient comparison above is restricted to the two covariates both models share.

2.2 Why this comparison matters

This reflects a pipeline design choice: use the array as the primary replication unit for community/joint models (Module 4+), while fitting single-species models at the finer camera level here. Point estimates generally keep a consistent sign between levels for well-detected species, but the array-level result for a sparse or heavily range-masked species should be treated as a much weaker signal than its p-value alone suggests.

There is also a more general ecological framework for why camera-level and array-level results can legitimately differ, not just statistically but biologically: Johnson’s (1980) hierarchy of habitat selection. Johnson observed that animals select habitat at nested spatial scales — from the geographic range down to the individual resource item — and that a habitat association measured at one scale doesn’t automatically transfer to another. An array-level occupancy model asks a second-order question: what determines where, across the broader landscape, a home range (here approximated by the array footprint) ends up detecting the species at all? A camera-level model asks a third-order question: given that a home range is already present, what fine-scale microhabitat features predict detection at this specific spot within it? These are genuinely different questions, and a covariate can matter at one order and not the other simply because it operates at a different spatial scale than the one being tested.

knitr::include_graphics(file.path(FIGS, "m3_johnson_levels_of_selection.png"))

3 Adding an interaction effect

We extend the occupancy model to let one habitat effect depend on another variable — here, whether the effect of tree cover on occupancy changes with temperature. This is fit as a full model, not an interaction term alone:

psi ~ tree_cover * temperature + savanna + pasture + cropland +
      native_veg_1000m + precipitation + built_surface_5000m +
      dist_road + dist_water + in_pa

Tree cover (a MapBiomas year-2000 baseline layer, distinct from the pipeline’s standard forest_100m covariate) substitutes for forest in this model, since the two are highly correlated (r = 0.82) and would otherwise create collinearity with the interaction term. All other covariates from the 11-covariate camera-level set remain in the model as ordinary additive effects.

knitr::include_graphics(file.path(FIGS, "m3_interaction_4species.png"))
i4 <- fread(file.path(DATA, "interaction_4species.csv"))
knitr::kable(i4[, .(common, interaction_coef, z)], digits=3,
  col.names=c("Species","Interaction coefficient","z"),
  caption="Temperature x tree-cover interaction term, full model, four species.")
Temperature x tree-cover interaction term, full model, four species.
Species Interaction coefficient z
Lowland Tapir -0.632 -3.66
Yellow Armadillo 17.804 1.63
Nine-banded Armadillo 0.693 3.86
Crab-eating Fox -0.620 -3.84

An interaction term is a useful extension when a single slope genuinely doesn’t capture the ecology — here, three of four species show a genuine, statistically supported tree-cover-by-temperature interaction even after controlling for the full covariate set, which an additive-only model would average away.

3.1 Does this interaction cluster by taxonomic order?

The four-species example above shows the interaction can matter a great deal for a handful of species. We extend this to the full community: fit the same interaction to every modeled species/genus, tag each by taxonomic order, and ask whether any order stands out — specifically, whether Xenarthra (armadillos, anteaters; thermal physiology closer to ectothermy than other placental mammals) shows a more pronounced temperature-dependence in its forest-use response than the rest of the community.

knitr::include_graphics(file.path(FIGS, "m3_interaction_by_order.png"))
osum <- fread(file.path(DATA, "order_interaction_summary.csv"))
knitr::kable(osum, digits=2, col.names=c("Order","N species","Mean |z|","Median |z|","% significant"),
  caption="Temperature x tree-cover interaction strength, by taxonomic order.")
Temperature x tree-cover interaction strength, by taxonomic order.
Order N species Mean |z| Median |z| % significant
Perissodactyla 1 3.66 3.66 100.00
Didelphimorphia 3 1.77 2.10 66.67
Xenarthra 5 1.77 1.63 40.00
Lagomorpha 1 1.56 1.56 0.00
Artiodactyla 4 1.36 1.33 0.00
Carnivora 12 1.33 0.95 25.00
Rodentia 5 1.04 1.25 20.00
Primates 1 0.01 0.01 0.00 
xt <- fread(file.path(DATA, "xenarthra_test.csv"))

Xenarthra’s mean |z| (1.77, n = 5) is somewhat higher than the rest of the community combined (1.37, n = 27), but a Wilcoxon rank-sum test finds no significant difference (p = 0.5448). With only 5 Xenarthra species in the modeled set, this test has limited power — the pattern is suggestive, not conclusive, and is a useful example for students of a hypothesis that is easy to state but hard to test cleanly with this sample size.

A single |z| number per species compresses away the shape of each interaction — two species can both have a large |z| while one shows a narrowing gap between cool and warm scenarios and the other shows a crossover. To compare shapes directly rather than just magnitudes, we plot the fitted cool-vs-warm prediction curves for the ten species/genera with the strongest interaction, all on a common scale:

knitr::include_graphics(file.path(FIGS, "m3_interaction_top10.png"))
top10 <- fread(file.path(DATA, "top10_interaction_species.csv"))
knitr::kable(top10, digits=2, col.names=c("Species/genus","Interaction z","Taxonomic order"),
  caption="The ten species/genera with the strongest temperature x tree-cover interaction, ranked by |z|.")
The ten species/genera with the strongest temperature x tree-cover interaction, ranked by |z|.
Species/genus Interaction z Taxonomic order
Dasypus novemcinctus 3.86 Xenarthra
Cerdocyon thous -3.84 Carnivora
Tapirus terrestris -3.66 Perissodactyla
Panthera onca 2.88 Carnivora

Nasua nasua 2.80 Carnivora

4 Letting a relationship vary by ecoregion

A different way habitat relationships can vary: not with a continuous covariate, but across ecologically distinct regions. We test this with Ocelot, comparing a single pooled forest effect against a full model that lets the forest effect differ between two ecoregions with enough data (at least six arrays each) — Moist Broadleaf Forest and the drier Grasslands/Savannas & Shrublands — while every other covariate stays in the model as an ordinary additive (fixed, not ecoregion-varying) effect:

psi ~ forest * ecoregion + savanna + pasture + cropland +
      native_veg_1000m + temperature + precipitation +
      built_surface_5000m + dist_road + dist_water + in_pa
eco <- fread(file.path(DATA, "ecoregion_ocelot_aic.csv"))
knitr::kable(eco, digits=1, col.names=c("\u0394AIC (interaction model favored)"),
  caption="AIC comparison: pooled forest effect vs. ecoregion-interaction model, full covariate set.")
AIC comparison: pooled forest effect vs. ecoregion-interaction model, full covariate set.
ΔAIC (interaction model favored)
6.6 
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(FIGS, "m3_ecoregion_ocelot.png"))

This is the same lesson as the temperature interaction, applied to a categorical rather than continuous moderator: a single “forest effect” number can hide two genuinely different relationships that only become visible once the data are split by ecological context.

5 Comparing to Royle-Nichols abundance

The Royle-Nichols model uses the same 1/0 detection data as occupancy, but interprets the frequency of detection across occasions as a signal of how many individuals are present at a site, not just whether the species is present at all.

knitr::include_graphics(file.path(FIGS, "m3_occ_vs_abundance.png"))
rnc <- fread(file.path(DATA, "rn_vs_occ_correlation.csv"))
knitr::kable(rnc, digits=2, col.names=c("Overall-level r","Forest-effect r","N Royle-Nichols fit","N modeled"),
  caption="Agreement between occupancy and Royle-Nichols abundance across the community.")
Agreement between occupancy and Royle-Nichols abundance across the community.
Overall-level r Forest-effect r N Royle-Nichols fit N modeled
0.83 0.82 33 33

Agreement is strong on overall level and solid on the forest effect specifically — a useful cross-check that the community model’s habitat signal is not an artifact of the occupancy framework’s binary detection assumption.

6 What the results mean

  • Every model in this module uses the range-masked candidate site set from Module 2’s range-map evaluation, and the 11-covariate camera-level / 6-covariate array-level split decided in Module 2’s data-driven covariate ranking.
  • Fixed-effects-only fitting is unreliable for roughly half the community due to separation; the array random-effect model resolves this by regularizing through the array intercept and is the pipeline’s default.
  • Forest cover is the community’s most consistent habitat signal; occupancy and Royle-Nichols abundance agree well on both overall level and the forest effect specifically, once unstable Royle-Nichols fits are excluded.
  • Collapsing cameras to arrays as the sampling unit — and the covariate set along with it — widens confidence intervals substantially, a real cost in statistical power, though point estimates mostly keep a consistent direction across the two levels.
  • Two extensions — a continuous interaction (temperature x tree cover) and a categorical one (ecoregion) — both show that a single “one number fits all” habitat effect can obscure real, ecologically sensible variation, fit as full models with the complete covariate set rather than the interaction term alone.
  • Testing the same temperature x tree-cover interaction across the whole community, grouped by taxonomic order, is a natural extension of the single-species interaction result — but with only five Xenarthra species in the modeled set, this is a sample-size-limited, suggestive test rather than a confirmed finding either way.
  • Protected-area status is a genuinely large effect for Nine-banded Armadillo: predicted occupancy inside protected areas is roughly half of predicted occupancy outside, holding other covariates at their mean.

We start with the **Nine-banded Armadillo** (*Dasypus novemcinctus*), a
well-detected species, and fit a model using every covariate in the

Occupancy models are built from a **detection history**: for each 7-day

```{r beta-table}
#| fig-cap: "Habitat effects on occupancy across the community, array random effect included, 11-covariate camera-level set. n_det = total detections, n_arr = arrays with a detection. A star marks a 95% credible interval that excludes zero. Green = positive, red = negative."
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(FIGS, "m3_beta_shaded_table.png"))
```

Forest is the most consistently important covariate across the community,
positive for the great majority of species with a credible effect.

## Does the array-level simplification hold?

Module 2 flagged that habitat is not always homogeneous within an array. We
test directly: does using arrays — rather than individual cameras — as the
sampling unit change the ecological conclusions? This is now a comparison of
**two genuinely different covariate sets**, not just two sampling levels
with the same covariates: the camera-level fit uses the full 11-covariate
set (1,110+ sites easily supports this); the array-level fit uses the
reduced 6-covariate set (60 arrays cannot support more; see Module 2 for how
that set was chosen).

Six species illustrate the comparison: Spotted Paca and Nine-banded
Armadillo (data-rich), White-lipped Peccary (sparser, range-masked), and
Ocelot, Lowland Tapir, and Puma (chosen for large camera-vs-array shifts).

```{r array-completeness}
ac <- fread(file.path(DATA, "array_completeness.csv"))
```

`r ac$n_arrays_complete` of `r ac$n_arrays_total` arrays have complete
covariate data for array-level models — one array has no valid camera-level
habitat data on any of its cameras and is dropped rather than silently
carried as an undefined average.

```{r array-vs-site}
#| fig-cap: "Camera-level (11 covariates) vs. array-level (6 covariates) occupancy coefficients and 95% confidence intervals, for the same six species, restricted to the two covariates both models share (forest and landscape-scale native vegetation). Confidence intervals widen sharply at the array level — fewer sampling units means less power."
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(FIGS, "m3_array_vs_site_6species.png"))
```

```{r camera-vs-array-fit}
#| fig-cap: "Model discrimination (AUC) at the camera level (11 covariates) vs. the array level (6 covariates), for the same six species. Array-level AUC is typically higher — fewer, cleaner sampling units are easier to discriminate, at the cost of much wider confidence intervals."
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(FIGS, "m3_camera_vs_array_fit_6species.png"))
```

```{r fitstats-6species-table}
fst <- fread(file.path(DATA, "fitstats_6species.csv"))
common_lookup6 <- c("Cuniculus paca"="Spotted Paca","Dasypus novemcinctus"="Nine-banded Armadillo",
                    "Tayassu pecari"="White-lipped Peccary","Leopardus pardalis"="Ocelot",
                    "Tapirus terrestris"="Lowland Tapir","Puma concolor"="Puma")
fst[, common := common_lookup6[species]]
knitr::kable(fst[, .(common, n_site, n_array, auc_site, auc_array)], digits=3,
  col.names=c("Species","N (camera-level)","N (array-level)","AUC (camera, 11 cov.)","AUC (array, 6 cov.)"),
  caption="Camera-level vs. array-level model-fit statistics, six species.")
```

Note that the camera-level model also carries four covariates — built-surface
extent, distance to road, distance to water, protected-area status — that
the array-level model has no room to include; the coefficient comparison
above is restricted to the two covariates both models share.

## Why this comparison matters

This reflects a pipeline design choice: use the array as the primary
replication unit for community/joint models (Module 4+), while fitting
single-species models at the finer camera level here. Point estimates
generally keep a consistent sign between levels for well-detected species,
but the array-level result for a sparse or heavily range-masked species
should be treated as a much weaker signal than its p-value alone suggests.

There is also a more general ecological framework for why camera-level and
array-level results can legitimately differ, not just statistically but
biologically: **Johnson's (1980) hierarchy of habitat selection**. Johnson
observed that animals select habitat at nested spatial scales — from the
geographic range down to the individual resource item — and that a habitat
association measured at one scale doesn't automatically transfer to another.
An **array-level** occupancy model asks a **second-order** question: what
determines *where*, across the broader landscape, a home range (here
approximated by the array footprint) ends up detecting the species at all?
A **camera-level** model asks a **third-order** question: given that a home
range is already present, what fine-scale microhabitat features predict
detection at *this specific spot* within it? These are genuinely different
questions, and a covariate can matter at one order and not the other simply
because it operates at a different spatial scale than the one being tested.

```{r johnson-levels-fig}
#| fig-cap: "Left: a single Snapshot Brasil array (14 cameras) illustrating the two spatial scales directly relevant to this module — the array as a whole (second-order selection) and the individual cameras within it (third-order selection). Right: Johnson's (1980) full four-level hierarchy of habitat selection, with the two orders this module models highlighted."
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(FIGS, "m3_johnson_levels_of_selection.png"))
```

## Species groupings from the coefficient table

```{r species-pca}
#| fig-cap: "Species grouped by their full habitat-response profile from the community model (11-covariate camera-level set, standardized). Four k-means groups emerge, visible as distinct clusters in the scatter."
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(FIGS, "m3_species_pca_biplot.png"))
```

# Adding an interaction effect

We extend the occupancy model to let one habitat effect depend on another
variable — here, whether the effect of tree cover on occupancy changes with
temperature. This is fit as a **full model**, not an interaction term alone:

```
psi ~ tree_cover * temperature + savanna + pasture + cropland +
      native_veg_1000m + precipitation + built_surface_5000m +
      dist_road + dist_water + in_pa
```

Tree cover (a MapBiomas year-2000 baseline layer, distinct from the
pipeline's standard `forest_100m` covariate) substitutes for forest in this
model, since the two are highly correlated (r = 0.82) and would otherwise
create collinearity with the interaction term. All other covariates from the
11-covariate camera-level set remain in the model as ordinary additive
effects.

```{r interaction-4species}
#| fig-cap: "Temperature x tree-cover interaction, full model (all other covariates included and held at their mean), with 95% confidence bands. Cool (blue), average (grey), and warm (red) temperature scenarios are plotted separately."
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(FIGS, "m3_interaction_4species.png"))
```

```{r interaction-4species-table}
i4 <- fread(file.path(DATA, "interaction_4species.csv"))
knitr::kable(i4[, .(common, interaction_coef, z)], digits=3,
  col.names=c("Species","Interaction coefficient","z"),
  caption="Temperature x tree-cover interaction term, full model, four species.")
```

An interaction term is a useful extension when a single slope genuinely
doesn't capture the ecology — here, three of four species show a genuine,
statistically supported tree-cover-by-temperature interaction even after
controlling for the full covariate set, which an additive-only model would
average away.

## Does this interaction cluster by taxonomic order?

The four-species example above shows the interaction can matter a great
deal for a handful of species. We extend this to the full community: fit
the *same* interaction to every modeled species/genus, tag each by
taxonomic order, and ask whether any order stands out — specifically,
whether **Xenarthra** (armadillos, anteaters; thermal physiology closer to
ectothermy than other placental mammals) shows a more pronounced
temperature-dependence in its forest-use response than the rest of the
community.

```{r order-interaction-fig}
#| fig-cap: "Temperature x tree-cover interaction strength (|z|), by taxonomic order. Each point is one species/genus; the black bar is the order mean; red points are Xenarthra."
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(FIGS, "m3_interaction_by_order.png"))
```

```{r order-interaction-table}
osum <- fread(file.path(DATA, "order_interaction_summary.csv"))
knitr::kable(osum, digits=2, col.names=c("Order","N species","Mean |z|","Median |z|","% significant"),
  caption="Temperature x tree-cover interaction strength, by taxonomic order.")
```

```{r xenarthra-test}
xt <- fread(file.path(DATA, "xenarthra_test.csv"))
```

Xenarthra's mean |z| (`r xt$mean_xenarthra`, n = `r xt$n_xenarthra`) is
somewhat higher than the rest of the community combined (`r xt$mean_other`,
n = `r xt$n_other`), but a Wilcoxon rank-sum test finds no significant
difference (p = `r xt$wilcoxon_p`). With only `r xt$n_xenarthra` Xenarthra
species in the modeled set, this test has limited power — the pattern is
suggestive, not conclusive, and is a useful example for students of a
hypothesis that is easy to state but hard to test cleanly with this sample
size.

A single |z| number per species compresses away the *shape* of each
interaction — two species can both have a large |z| while one shows a
narrowing gap between cool and warm scenarios and the other shows a
crossover. To compare shapes directly rather than just magnitudes, we plot
the fitted cool-vs-warm prediction curves for the ten species/genera with
the strongest interaction, all on a common scale:

```{r top10-interactions}
#| fig-cap: "The ten strongest temperature x tree-cover interactions, compared directly by their fitted cool-vs-warm prediction curves rather than by |z| alone. Each panel is one species/genus, ordered by interaction strength; the taxonomic order and z-value are given in each panel's label."
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(FIGS, "m3_interaction_top10.png"))
```

```{r top10-table}
top10 <- fread(file.path(DATA, "top10_interaction_species.csv"))
knitr::kable(top10, digits=2, col.names=c("Species/genus","Interaction z","Taxonomic order"),
  caption="The ten species/genera with the strongest temperature x tree-cover interaction, ranked by |z|.")
```

# Letting a relationship vary by ecoregion

A different way habitat relationships can vary: not with a continuous
covariate, but across ecologically distinct regions. We test this with
**Ocelot**, comparing a single pooled forest effect against a **full model**
that lets the forest effect differ between two ecoregions with enough data
(at least six arrays each) — Moist Broadleaf Forest and the drier
Grasslands/Savannas & Shrublands — while every other covariate stays in the
model as an ordinary additive (fixed, not ecoregion-varying) effect:

```
psi ~ forest * ecoregion + savanna + pasture + cropland +
      native_veg_1000m + temperature + precipitation +
      built_surface_5000m + dist_road + dist_water + in_pa
```

```{r ecoregion-aic}
eco <- fread(file.path(DATA, "ecoregion_ocelot_aic.csv"))
knitr::kable(eco, digits=1, col.names=c("\u0394AIC (interaction model favored)"),
  caption="AIC comparison: pooled forest effect vs. ecoregion-interaction model, full covariate set.")
```

```{r ecoregion-fig}
#| fig-cap: "Ocelot occupancy as a function of forest cover, fit separately by ecoregion (full model, other covariates fixed at their mean), with 95% confidence bands. In Moist Broadleaf Forest, more forest cover means more Ocelot occupancy. In Grasslands/Savannas & Shrublands the relationship reverses direction."
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(FIGS, "m3_ecoregion_ocelot.png"))
```

This is the same lesson as the temperature interaction, applied to a
categorical rather than continuous moderator: a single "forest effect"
number can hide two genuinely different relationships that only become
visible once the data are split by ecological context.

# Comparing to Royle-Nichols abundance

The **Royle-Nichols model** uses the same 1/0 detection data as occupancy,
but interprets the *frequency* of detection across occasions as a signal of
how many individuals are present at a site, not just whether the species is
present at all.

```{r rn-vs-occ}
#| fig-cap: "Left: mean occupancy (\u03c8-hat) vs. mean Royle-Nichols relative abundance (\u03bb-hat) across the community. Right: forest effect estimated two ways — standard occupancy vs. Royle-Nichols abundance. Unstable Royle-Nichols fits are excluded from both panels."
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(FIGS, "m3_occ_vs_abundance.png"))
```

```{r rn-correlation}
rnc <- fread(file.path(DATA, "rn_vs_occ_correlation.csv"))
knitr::kable(rnc, digits=2, col.names=c("Overall-level r","Forest-effect r","N Royle-Nichols fit","N modeled"),
  caption="Agreement between occupancy and Royle-Nichols abundance across the community.")
```

Agreement is strong on overall level and solid on the forest effect
specifically — a useful cross-check that the community model's habitat
signal is not an artifact of the occupancy framework's binary detection
assumption.

# What the results mean

- Every model in this module uses the range-masked candidate site set from
  Module 2's range-map evaluation, and the 11-covariate camera-level /
  6-covariate array-level split decided in Module 2's data-driven covariate
  ranking.
- Fixed-effects-only fitting is unreliable for roughly half the community
  due to separation; the array random-effect model resolves this by
  regularizing through the array intercept and is the pipeline's default.
- Forest cover is the community's most consistent habitat signal; occupancy
  and Royle-Nichols abundance agree well on both overall level and the
  forest effect specifically, once unstable Royle-Nichols fits are excluded.
- Collapsing cameras to arrays as the sampling unit — and the covariate set
  along with it — widens confidence intervals substantially, a real cost in
  statistical power, though point estimates mostly keep a consistent
  direction across the two levels.
- Two extensions — a continuous interaction (temperature x tree cover) and a
  categorical one (ecoregion) — both show that a single "one number fits
  all" habitat effect can obscure real, ecologically sensible variation, fit
  as full models with the complete covariate set rather than the
  interaction term alone.
- Testing the same temperature x tree-cover interaction across the whole
  community, grouped by taxonomic order, is a natural extension of the
  single-species interaction result — but with only five Xenarthra species
  in the modeled set, this is a sample-size-limited, suggestive test rather
  than a confirmed finding either way.
- Protected-area status is a genuinely large effect for Nine-banded
  Armadillo: predicted occupancy inside protected areas is roughly half of
  predicted occupancy outside, holding other covariates at their mean.
